transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 1:08
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (Redwood Infra SE), Ravi K (AtlasML CTO), Marta S (Lead ML Eng), Lina G (Platform Eng), Evan P (Research Eng)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on MoE routing costs, RoPE scaling behavior across Llama/Mistral/Qwen family, quantization tradeoffs (4-bit vs 8-bit), and on-prem/VPC implications for KV cache and batching. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share scripts and gating-cost spreadsheet; AtlasML to run targeted throughput and tail-latency tests.

Topics: MoE gating cost, expert memory reservation, rope (RoPE) scaling artifacts, KV cache sharding, int4/4-bit quantization pitfalls, continuous batching, Triton kernel choices, VPC peering for on-prem Redwood Private.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you all making time. Quick roll call — we got AtlasML on?
[00:08] Ravi Kapoor: Yep, here, Ravi. Marta's on, Lina, Evan. Thanks.
[00:12] Jordan Lee: Awesome. Priya and Marcus from our side, I'll hand it to Priya to frame the agenda.
[00:18] Priya Shah: Cool — hi all. We'll focus on three things: MoE routing costs and gating, RoPE scaling oddities we've seen on long-form context, and practical quantization/throughput tradeoffs when you run on prem or inside a VPC. Also leave time for infra questions. Sound good?
[00:30] Marta Silva: Sounds perfect. We ran some early tests with a 64k context and saw weird attention drift near 32k, thought that might be RoPE.
[00:38] Priya Shah: Yep, that's consistent with RoPE aliasing — sometimes shows up as attention wrap-around when absolute position encodings get large. With Llama-style rotary embeddings you can get periodicity unless you rescale or apply RoPE scaling.
[00:50] Marcus Chen: Can you clarify rescale? Like linear rescaling vs NTK-aware scaling?
[00:54] Priya Shah: Right. There are two pragmatic options we use: 1) linear position-id rescaling (a simple multiplicative factor to shift the frequency) and 2) NTK-scaled RoPE (reduce the effective frequency growth). For Mistral we've seen better stability with NTK-style adjustments, for Llama forks it's hit or miss. Qwen had some variations in the implementation that change the breakpoints.
[01:12] Marta Silva: So is that something we need to recompile into the model weights or can it be done in the runtime?
[01:18] Priya Shah: Good question — small rescale factors can be applied at runtime in the kernel (we've patched FlashAttention kernels to accept a scale param). For larger structural changes you'd have to patch the model. Runtime adjustments are lower-risk and preferred for POC.
[01:28] Evan Park: If we do runtime scaling, does that impact KV caching semantics? Like will cache keys be invalidated across scale changes?
[01:34] Priya Shah: It can. If the key/query projection uses positional multipliers that change across requests, the cached K/V won't match. Our approach is to version the cache per RoPE config (cache key includes rope_scale). So if you change scaling mid-session you flush or create a new cache bucket. Adds memory overhead but avoids corruption.
[01:51] Lina Gomez: Memory overhead is a concern for us on-prem; we can't just double KV cache. How do you size for MoE with many experts?
[01:58] Marcus Chen: Yeah we're trying to support a 32-expert MoE on an 80GB A100, per-GPU. How do you reserve memory for expert activations vs KV?
[02:06] Priya Shah: MoE is tricky. We separate two kinds of memory reservations: expert parameter memory (the expert weights) which is mostly static, and transient expert activation buffers which depend on batch size and gating sparsity. For training you'd keep lots of activation buffers, but for inference you can stream expert outputs and free quickly. Still, worst-case gating (many tokens routed to many experts) will spike memory. We recommend configuring a gating cap — e.g., max tokens per expert per batch — and have fallback routing to a generalist expert or smaller dense model to bound memory.
[02:33] Marta Silva: Can you explain gating cost calculation? We saw routing doubles latency in some of our tests.
[02:38] Priya Shah: Sure, gating cost has two main components: 1) compute overhead to run the gating network per-token (tiny but nonzero), and 2) the scatter/gather cost that arises when you move token activations across device memory to the chosen expert. The second dominates at scale: cross-GPU shuffles or additional memcpy to local expert buffers. If experts live on the same device as batching you avoid inter-GPU comms, but if not you pay NCCL or PCIe traffic.
[03:00] Jordan Lee: For many customers we adopt a route of collocating experts with the routing microshard so the scatter is local. That reduces routing latency but increases GPU memory footprint since every device needs a copy of the experts. It's a cost vs latency tradeoff.
[03:12] Ravi Kapoor: If we replicate experts, what's the economic hit? Like throughput per GPU drops?
[03:16] Priya Shah: You trade off some effective model parallel capacity. If you replicate all experts per-GPU you need more GPUs to reach same model parameter capacity. But the latency per request can fall dramatically because you avoid shuffles. We'll send a small spreadsheet that models the cost — it factors in replication factor, requests/sec, average experts per token, and egress.
[03:32] Marta Silva: We'll need that spreadsheet. Also curious about quantization — we tried int8 and saw hallucinations increase for Qwen. Any tips?
[03:40] Priya Shah: Qwen seems particularly sensitive to symmetric int8 in certain linear layers. For inference we recommend hybrid quant: 4-bit (GPTQ or AWQ style) for feed-forward weights, keep LayerNorms and some projection matrices in float16 or int8 with per-channel scales. For Qwen we prefer 4-bit with per-channel scaling + outlier handling. Also do a small eval suite — some of our customers use a set of 1000 critical prompts to measure delta in factuality before pushing quantized models.
[04:04] Evan Park: We use a prompt-heavy, short-response workload mostly. Sequence lengths average 512 but we have long-form batches for summarization up to 20k. How should we pick quant levels?
[04:12] Priya Shah: Keep long-form generation in higher precision (fp16) if accuracy is critical. For high throughput short responses, int4 is often fine. Redwood Optimize can suggest per-route quantization, so you can run the same model at different precisions per API route.
[04:25] Marta Silva: Does Redwood support dynamic precision at runtime? Like route short requests to quantized model and long requests to non-quantized?
[04:31] Jordan Lee: Yes — routing policies can pick model variant per-request. It's part of the smart routing piece. We'll note that down as a recommended pattern for AtlasML.
[04:38] Lina Gomez: On the VPC side: if we run Redwood Private inside our VPC, how do you handle KV cache persistence and network egress? We want to keep data residency internal.
[04:46] Marcus Chen: We currently support an on-prem package that keeps KV cache local to the customer's cluster; for VPC we do an option where cache lives in a customer-managed redis cluster or a sharded local disk. We avoid cross-AZ egress for the hot KV path. The control plane can be private-only as well.
[04:58] Lina Gomez: How about KMS/HSM integration for model keys?
[05:02] Priya Shah: We support KMS integration — AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and an HSM option for Private deployments. We recommend putting model decryption keys behind HSM if you're on-prem and regulated.
[05:12] Ravi Kapoor: Back to MoE routing: you mentioned gating caps and fallbacks — what are typical SLO parameters you recommend?
[05:18] Priya Shah: For latency-sensitive routes we aim for p95 < 120ms for short responses. To hit that with MoE we often set gating to limit to 1-2 experts per token, and use a small dense fallback (a distilled 8B) when gating would exceed thresholds. For high-throughput batch jobs, you can allow 4+ experts and process asynchronously.
[05:38] Marta Silva: We saw tail spikes during bursts; is continuous batching helpful?
[05:44] Marcus Chen: Continuous batching helps amortize per-batch kernel launch cost and increases throughput, but it can increase tail latency if greedy. Redwood's runtime implements workload-aware batching: it tries to batch to a latency budget and flushes partial batches beyond a timeout threshold. You can tune that flush_timeout per route.
[06:02] Evan Park: Any specific kernel choices for Llama vs Mistral? We saw FlashAttention2 vs vendor Triton perf differences.
[06:10] Priya Shah: FlashAttention2 with fused qkv kernels and custom RoPE handling tends to be best on Ampere and Hopper for long contexts, but Triton autotuned kernels sometimes win on short sequences. We maintain a kernel selector that picks based on seq_len distribution and hardware. For Mistral, its wider FFN shapes change the memory access pattern — sometimes a custom fused FFN kernel is huge win.
[06:34] Marta Silva: Interesting — about RoPE artifacts: we saw attention 'wrap-around' after a certain position, how do you detect and mitigate in prod?
[06:42] Priya Shah: Detect by running attention heatmaps across positions for representative prompts; if you see periodic spikes it's RoPE aliasing. Mitigate by scaling positions, or switch to relative position bias if model/weights support it. We can also apply a runtime windowing scheme for very long contexts to prevent wrap.
[06:57] Jordan Lee: Quick comment: sometimes the 'wrap' is mis-attributed — it's a combination of RoPE and KV cache eviction patterns. If older K/V are evicted or compressed differently you might see weird recency effects.
[07:08] Lina Gomez: You mentioned KV cache sharding earlier — can you explain the tradeoffs between sharding by token range vs shard-by-model-slice?
[07:14] Priya Shah: Sure. Shard-by-token-range (time-based) keeps KVs for contiguous segments on same shard; good for sequential long contexts but bad for random access. Shard-by-model-slice (e.g., head or attention-slice) means each shard holds part of K/V for all tokens; good for parallel compute but requires reassembly during decode. Token-range shards are easier for eviction policies; slice-shards can enable higher throughput if you co-locate compute. Depends on your workload and failure domains.
[07:42] Marta Silva: For our on-prem cluster, which approach do you recommend?
[07:45] Marcus Chen: For AtlasML's use case (mixed short + periodic long-form), we suggest token-range sharding with a hot-disk tier for the last N tokens and LRU eviction beyond that. Keeps memory bounded and minimizes cross-node traffic for most sessions.
[07:58] Evan Park: About quantization again — you mentioned AWQ/GPTQ — do you have a recommended toolchain? We prefer open-source.
[08:04] Priya Shah: For open-source toolchain, many teams use GPTQ for 4-bit static quant and AWQ for better symmetric handling; we also have internal scripts that re-scale outliers and recompute biases to reduce distribution shift. We'll include those sample scripts.
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Also note that for Qwen we saw better fidelity when keeping the q_proj and k_proj in higher precision — those are fragile.
[08:29] Marta Silva: Good to know.
[08:31] Lina Gomez: One last infra question: in a Private deployment behind our firewall, does Redwood still need any egress to control plane?
[08:38] Marcus Chen: There are two modes: fully air-gapped (control plane local) or hybrid where control plane is hosted and agents poll. For regulated customers we can do a private control plane inside your VPC, so no outbound egress required beyond your internal network.
[08:52] Ravi Kapoor: That would be necessary for our compliance team. We'll need SOC2/ISO docs.
[08:56] Jordan Lee: We'll send SOC2 type II + architecture diagram and a checklist for on-prem.
[09:02] Priya Shah: Back to perf — practical suggestion: run three microbenchmarks: 1) short-prompt p95 latency at 1 RPS to measure cold kernel path; 2) 1000 QPS steady state throughput test with gating enabled and disabled; 3) long-form rolling generate with context growth to 20k to verify RoPE and KV eviction. We'll provide the test harness.
[09:22] Marta Silva: We'll run those. For the 1000 QPS test, what environment do you recommend? Single node or multi-node?
[09:28] Priya Shah: Multi-node with collocated experts if you want low latency. Start single-node for baseline, then scale to multi-node to measure routing overhead. We'll include sample cluster configs.
[09:37] Evan Park: Anything else about model architecture tuning? Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen — high-level takeaways?
[09:43] Priya Shah: Llama variants generally are stable with RoPE patches and have predictable latency. Mistral's FFN shapes benefit from fused kernels and sometimes need different batching parameters. Qwen is more sensitive to quantization and some projection matrices; handle q/k projections with care. MoE adds routing complexity regardless of base architecture — gating network design and expert placement dominate cost.
[10:01] Jordan Lee: And from the infra side, pick your knobs: replicate experts for latency, shard experts for cost, cap gating to control memory, and route long contexts to higher precision.
[10:12] Marta Silva: This is great. Can you share the binder of configs?
[10:16] Priya Shah: Yes we'll share the gating spreadsheet, Triton and FlashAttention2 sample kernel flags, and a small-bench harness link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/atlasml-moe-tests (internal). Also a private doc with config examples: deck: redwood_moe_tuning.pdf
[10:30] Evan Park: On evaluation, we want to quantify hallucination delta after quantization. Any simple metrics?
[10:35] Priya Shah: Use precision/recall on factoid QA sets and a small set of human-labelled checks. We also monitor answer length, repetition, and confidence tokens as heuristics. For enterprise we tie quant deltas into a regression alert pipeline.
[10:48] Marta Silva: Ok makes sense.
[10:50] Jordan Lee: We're nearing the hour mark — quick recap and next steps. Priya?
[10:55] Priya Shah: Recap: Redwood to share MoE routing cost calc + gating spreadsheet, sample Triton and FlashAttention kernel flags, quant scripts (GPTQ/AWQ tips), and perf harness. AtlasML to run three benchmarks (short latency, throughput with gating on/off, long-form RoPE roll-up) and share prompt distributions and sequence lengths. Align on on-prem control plane requirements and SOC2 docs. We'll tentatively schedule an on-prem pilot kickoff week of 2025-03-17.
[11:20] Ravi Kapoor: Sounds good. Marta, Lina — anything to add?
[11:25] Marta Silva: No, just excited to try the harness. We'll prioritise the throughput test.
[11:29] Lina Gomez: I'll check firewall rules and follow up on peering.
[11:32] Jordan Lee: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the files and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[11:38] Ravi Kapoor: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
